samples.question: A thin horizontal rule runs across the full width of this image. Above the rule stands a single reference rail: a solid horizontal bar with one small square marker floating just above it. Below the rule stand five candidate rails of the same kind, one per row; count them 1 to 5 from top to bottom. Every rail is a straight bar of the same thickness and the same colour, and every rail carries exactly one marker. The six rails have different lengths and each one begins at its own horizontal position on the page, so the rails are not aligned with one another. For any rail, read its marker's position as the distance from that rail's own left end to the centre of its marker, divided by that same rail's own full length: that is the marker's fraction along its rail, and it does not change if the rail is moved sideways or if the whole rail with its marker is scaled up or down. Exactly one candidate rail places its marker at the same fraction along its own length as the reference rail does along the reference length. In every other candidate rail that fraction differs from the reference fraction by at least ten percent of the rail's length, so no comparison is a close call. Absolute pixel measurements are traps and are not the rule: one of the wrong rails puts its marker exactly the same number of pixels from its own left end as the reference does, in the very same screen column, and another wrong rail has exactly the same total length as the reference rail, while the correct rail has a different length and a different absolute marker offset from the reference. Rail length, rail starting position, the amount of ink, marker size and colour therefore carry no information; only the fraction does. Where in the stack below the rule is the rail whose marker sits at the same fraction of its own length as the reference marker? Answer with exactly one of: topmost, second-from-top, middle, fourth-from-top, bottommost.
